title: From algebra to engineering
kicker: THE FOUNDATIONS HAVE SOMEWHERE TO GO
description: Start with quantities you can hold, then give equations a physical job. Fractions become clearances, functions become machine behavior, and calculus becomes a way to track motion and accumulation. Follow the sequence or revisit the idea your current class is making difficult.
destination: Build a model you can explain.
projectIdea: Make a spreadsheet for a fictional service tank: choose an initial quantity, an inflow, and an outflow; show the remaining quantity over time. Label every unit, find when a chosen threshold is reached, and explain how the answer changes when one rate changes. Keep a hand calculation beside the graph.

title: Make the motion work
kicker: FROM A DRAWING TO A MECHANISM
description: Follow a load through a hinge, gear, or bracket. Learn to describe the shape, predict the forces, and account for the small dimensional differences that decide whether parts fit. The destination is a mechanism study with measurements someone else can inspect.
destination: Turn a simple hinge into an engineering study.
projectIdea: Sketch a small cardboard hinge or lever with two views and a reference dimension. Predict how changing the lever arm changes the required force, compare two low-force arrangements, and record the geometry and observations. Add a paper tolerance stack to show how clearance could vary before making another version.

title: Give a robot a useful job
description: Begin with where a tool can reach, then ask how it moves and how it knows whether the task is finished. Connect coordinates, force, algorithms, and feedback through a simple arm or cart. Each step adds a piece of reasoning you can use when a mechanism behaves differently from its drawing.
destination: Make a paper arm reach a defined target.
projectIdea: Build a two-link paper arm with marked joint centers. Predict its tip position, compare that prediction with a ruler measurement, and record the error. Write a short procedure that declares success using a stated position tolerance, then trace how a feedback rule would correct an invented measurement error.

title: Learn to think in orbits
kicker: FROM A PUSH TO A TRAJECTORY
description: Start with inertia and changing velocity, then follow energy through a trajectory. See why a forward push can eventually lead to a slower circular orbit, and why a rotating habitat is another acceleration problem. The route joins familiar classroom quantities to motion on a much larger scale.
destination: Explain the whole trajectory, not just the burn.
projectIdea: Draw an inner circle, an outer circle, and a transfer ellipse. Mark the two velocity changes and calculate the four endpoint speeds from the orbital-transfer lesson. Add a separate rotation study showing how radius and spin rate affect floor acceleration. Use sketches and units to explain why the two problems both involve curved motion.

title: Keep a place alive and working
description: A habitat is a set of flows and boundaries before it becomes a skyline. Connect algebra to water inventory, geometry to usable space, and energy conservation to cooling. Then look for the shared dependencies that can defeat an apparently redundant arrangement.
destination: Give every flow a source and a destination.
projectIdea: Make a one-page diagram of a fictional small habitat with water, electrical, and heat flows. Give each selected device an operating mode, calculate one day's energy demand from power and time, and trace the heat to an external sink. Cross out one shared dependency and explain which services remain available.

title: Take the engineering underwater
description: Water changes the loads, the access, and the questions you ask of a machine. Use hydrostatic pressure to connect depth with a wall load, then follow that load through a structure. Continue into remote manipulation, measurement, and tests that separate the design from the conditions around it.
destination: Design the evidence for an ocean instrument.
projectIdea: On paper, choose a depth and a simple instrument enclosure. Calculate the outside pressure and the pressure difference across one small horizontal face, then sketch the resulting load path. Add an access sketch for a remote tool and a proposed inspection plan. Keep the pressure calculation, structural questions, and serviceability questions distinct.

title: Make a decision worth trusting
description: Good engineering judgment grows from clear comparisons and honest communication. Learn to see variation, avoid a misleading test, and write a decision another person can challenge. History, ethics, economics, and teamwork become practical tools when the next step affects someone else's work.
destination: Run a small review with real evidence.
projectIdea: Compare two harmless tabletop task layouts. Define the task, vary their order, record the conditions and completion times, and preserve inconvenient observations. Write a one-page recommendation that separates measurements from interpretation, names the cost of the next test, and states what evidence would change your recommendation.

title: Read the signal. Shape the response.
kicker: FROM FUNCTIONS TO A FEEDBACK LOOP
description: Follow a number as it becomes a time-varying signal, a measurement, and a correction. Build the geometry behind phase, use calculus to describe change and accumulation, and trace a feedback rule step by step. The emphasis stays on understanding what the model and the data actually say.
destination: Build a controller you can inspect one step at a time.
projectIdea: Create a spreadsheet with reference, measured position, error, gain, and next position. Compare three gains using the same starting condition, then introduce an invented sensor offset and explain the difference between measured success and actual position. Add an input check that keeps missing readings separate from valid zeros.
